body:
Lynch caddied for Fidelity's president as a teenager, bought Flying Tiger in college for his first tenbagger, and joined Fidelity as an analyst ([PBS Frontline](https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/pages/frontline/shows/betting/pros/lynch.html)). Magellan was about **$20 million when he took over in 1977 and $14 billion when he left** ([PBS Frontline](https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/pages/frontline/shows/betting/pros/lynch.html)). It returned about **29.2% a year against the market's 15.5%** on CRSP data ([CapexCat](https://capexcat.substack.com/p/peter-lynch-buy-what-you-know)), or 26.4% against 13.3% on CBS's measure ([CBS MoneyWatch](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/lessons-from-a-great-fund-managers-record)). The best years came while the fund was small and closed to new money, until 1981.

The workload is the part nobody copies. Lynch arrived around 6:45 a.m., stayed about 13 hours, worked Saturdays, spent a week a month on the road, and made **200+ company visits while reading about 700 annual reports a year**. First-year turnover was 343%, and the fund eventually held about 1,400 stocks ([CapexCat](https://capexcat.substack.com/p/peter-lynch-buy-what-you-know)). In his own words: "I was working six days a week and that wasn't even enough… I could see any company I wanted to see" ([PBS Frontline](https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/pages/frontline/shows/betting/pros/lynch.html)). That open access to management existed before Regulation FD curbed selective disclosure in 2000. His biggest bets were unpopular. He held Chrysler near bankruptcy as his largest position while people asked "Don't you know they're going bankrupt?" He also credited luck openly. He retired at 46 because "it was just too much time." After he left, Magellan at $14–50 billion returned 7.8% a year and trailed the S&P ([CBS MoneyWatch](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/lessons-from-a-great-fund-managers-record)). "Buy what you know" is a distortion. He says he never told people to invest on that basis, and his fuller line is "know what you own" ([Yahoo Finance](https://ca.finance.yahoo.com/news/fidelity-legend-peter-lynch-i-never-said-to-invest-in-the-stock-market-120755736.html)).

body: **Summary:** NBFCs borrow wholesale (bank loans, NCDs, CP) and lend to niches banks under-serve: consumer durables, vehicle, gold, MSME, affordable housing and microfinance. Spread minus opex minus credit cost gives RoA, typically 2–4% for the best players and ~1.5–2.5% for HFCs, levered 4–7x. Key metrics: AUM growth, NIM/spread, cost of funds and ALM gaps, credit cost, GS3/NS3 plus Stage-2, opex/AUM, RoA, capital adequacy, borrowing mix. Cycle drivers are wholesale funding cost and availability (IL&FS Sep 2018, DHFL 2019), RBI risk-weight changes (Nov 2023), and segment stress such as microfinance over-indebtedness in FY25–26. Lead indicators: RBI NBFC credit data, CP and CD spreads, MFIN Micrometer, CRIF reports, NHB and rating-agency sector notes. Winners (Bajaj Finance, Cholamandalam, Muthoot) had a granular book, a diversified funding base, data-led underwriting and parentage or access to cheap capital. Losers (DHFL, IL&FS, Reliance Capital, several MFIs) borrowed short to lend long, had related-party exposures, or chased growth in one hot segment. Valuation: P/B against RoE and growth runway. Bajaj Finance traded at about 6–10x book at its 2019–21 peak; vehicle and gold lenders trade at 1.5–3.5x. Nov 2026: NBFC credit grew 15.4% YoY in Sep 2026 (RBI), Bajaj Finance AUM reached ₹5.85 lakh cr (+26.5%), and ICRA moved its MFI outlook to Stable. Traps: ignoring ALM, and treating low credit costs in an upcycle as permanent. Sources: [1](https://rbi.org.in/SCRIPTs/BS_PressReleaseDisplay.aspx?prid=63940) · [2](https://www.venturasecurities.com/?p=65123) · [3](https://www.icra.in/Research/ViewResearchReport/7150) · [4](https://www.multibagg.ai/market-pulse/articles/aditya-birla-capital-nbfc-growth-ppt-cmvuuacpw002x2klzlxzxpkk6) · [5](https://www.newkerala.com/news/a/hfcs-emerge-stronger-after-fy26-stress-asset-quality-215.htm)

body: `insight:valuation-method-by-sector` · confidence: unverified Use the metric that tracks how each sector creates value. A P/E applied to the wrong sector misleads. Lenders (banks, NBFCs, HFCs): P/B against sustainable RoE, where justified P/B = (RoE−g)/(CoE−g). A 2x-book bank with 17% RoE is cheaper than a 1x bank whose RoA is falling. Life insurers: P/EV and implied VNB multiple; ignore P/E, because new business strain depresses reported profit. AMCs and exchanges: P/E plus % of AUM, adjusting for peak volumes. Cyclicals (metals, cement, CVs, chemicals): EV/EBITDA on mid-cycle margins, or EV per tonne against replacement cost (cement $80–120/t). Never use spot P/E, because P/E is lowest at peak earnings. Capital goods and EPC: P/E plus order-book cover and OCF conversion. Utilities: P/B against regulated RoE (~15.5% CERC); renewables on EV/EBITDA and equity IRR against cost of equity. Real estate: P/NAV and presales/OCF; reported P/E is meaningless under completion accounting. Consumer franchises (FMCG, alcobev, retail): P/E or reverse DCF. Ask what volume growth the price implies (a 60x P/E needs ~15%+ earnings growth for 10+ years). Retail and QSR: pre-Ind AS 116 EV/EBITDA, because the lease standard flatters EBITDA. Pharma: P/E excluding one-off exclusivity profits, with a sum of parts for India branded, US and CDMO. EMS: EV/EBITDA and RoCE, not P/sales, since the margin is thin and the revenue pass-through. Defence: P/E against order-book-driven earnings growth (PEG), because order books lift visibility but not margin. **rule_table:** - banks/NBFC: P/B vs RoE - life insurance: P/EV - AMC/exchanges: P/E, %AUM - metals/cement/chemicals/CV: EV/EBITDA mid-cycle, EV/t - cap goods/EPC: P/E + order cover + OCF - utilities: P/B vs regulated RoE - renewables: EV/EBITDA, equity IRR - real estate: P/NAV, presales/OCF - FMCG/alcobev: P/E + reverse DCF - retail/QSR: pre-Ind AS EV/EBITDA - pharma: P/E ex one-offs, SOTP - EMS: EV/EBITDA + RoCE - defence: P/E vs order-led growth **lesson:** Pick the metric that tracks how the sector creates value; P/E is wrong for lenders, insurers, developers and cyclicals at extremes. Sources: [1](https://www.indexpe.in/blog/nifty-sector-valuations-june-2026) · [2](https://tapetide.com/insight/market-valuation) · [3](https://plindia.com/ResReport/Quant-3-11-26-PL.pdf) Links: about `theme:sector-private-banks`, about `theme:sector-nbfc-hfc`, about `theme:sector-insurance`, about `theme:sector-amc-capital-markets`, about `theme:sector-it-services`, about `theme:sector-pharma-cdmo`, about `theme:sector-specialty-chemicals`, about `theme:sector-auto-oems`

body:
**What worked**
- **Rule zero pointed straight at L5.** Listing the five most-asked questions showed that nobody models the parent take. That led to the support-services doubling and the royalty renewal date within the first two hours.
- **L13 ("boring filings") held again**, this time through other-expenses note 31, RPT note 41, the BRSR and the AGM-notice annex.
- **Techniques #10 (definition audit) and #12 (physics check) transferred unchanged** to "DC = 30–40%" and "equivalent units".
- The override table format worked, and so did the "looks good" rows: ROCE, utilisation, exports, other income.

**What was missing for a manufacturer (vs a retailer)**
1. **Unit definition.** A manufacturer has three units (plant, product node, channel account). The protocol assumed one (the store).
2. **The L4 default was wage-centred.** It must be chosen by cost weight. Materials were 63% of sales here; wages at minimum-wage level were 0.3%.
3. **No commodity pass-through method.** There was no routine for the materials ratio by quarter, cost-plus pass-in vs contracted pass-out, inventory cost layers, lag estimation, or leading price series.
4. **No MNC parent-take layer:** royalty, support/cost allocations, transfer-pricing formulas, purchases from and sales to group companies, dividends to the parent, and renewal dates. The AGM-notice RPT annex (SEBI Jun-2025 standard) was not listed as a source.
5. **BRSR physical-output intensity → volume** was not a listed technique.
6. **The customer-concentration footnote (Ind AS 108)** and the **other-income decomposition** (treasury, group rent, JV dividends → core PBT) were not in L2.
7. **No regulatory-transition template** (emission norms, BIS/QCOs, labour codes).
8. **Capacity:** own-plant vs group/supplier capacity was not distinguished.
9. **B2B scuttlebutt rules:** the L6 rules were store-centric (footfall, bills). B2B needs price sheets by node, lead times, a parts-price basket and tender results.
10. **Tool note:** `nse_fetch.py transcripts --download` ignores date filters. Listing first and then curling the needed URLs saved time.
